claim: DNA base damage arises frequently in living cells and needs to be removed by base excision repair (BER) to prevent mutagenesis and genome instability.
source: DNA base damage arises frequently in living cells and needs to be removed by base excision repair (BER) to prevent mutagenesis and genome instability.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DNA damage and repair mechanisms.

claim: Both the formation and repair of base damage occur in chromatin and are conceivably affected by DNA-binding proteins such as transcription factors (TFs).
source: Both the formation and repair of base damage occur in chromatin and are conceivably affected by DNA-binding proteins such as transcription factors (TFs).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential effects of TFs on damage and repair.

claim: Alkylation damage formation was mainly suppressed at the binding sites of yeast TFs Abf1 and Reb1.
source: Our data show that alkylation damage formation was mainly suppressed at the binding sites of yeast TFs ARS binding factor 1 (Abf1) and rDNA enhancer binding protein 1 (Reb1), but individual hotspots with elevated damage levels were also found.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Individual hotspots with elevated damage levels were found at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites.
source: Our data show that alkylation damage formation was mainly suppressed at the binding sites of yeast TFs ARS binding factor 1 (Abf1) and rDNA enhancer binding protein 1 (Reb1), but individual hotspots with elevated damage levels were also found.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Abf1 and Reb1 binding strongly inhibits BER in vivo and in vitro.
source: Additionally, Abf1 and Reb1 binding strongly inhibits BER in vivo and in vitro, causing slow repair both within the core motif and its adjacent DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by both cellular NMP-seq data and in vitro repair assays.

claim: TF binding causes slow repair both within the core motif and its adjacent DNA.
source: Additionally, Abf1 and Reb1 binding strongly inhibits BER in vivo and in vitro, causing slow repair both within the core motif and its adjacent DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data showing repair kinetics at TF binding sites.

claim: Repair of ultraviolet (UV) damage by nucleotide excision repair (NER) was inhibited by TF binding.
source: Repair of ultraviolet (UV) damage by nucleotide excision repair (NER) was also inhibited by TF binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by CPD-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TF binding inhibits a larger DNA region for NER relative to BER.
source: Interestingly, TF binding inhibits a larger DNA region for NER relative to BER.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of CPD-seq and NMP-seq data at TF binding sites.

claim: Damage formation and BER can be restored by depletion of Abf1 or Reb1 protein from the nucleus.
source: The observed effects are caused by the TF–DNA interaction, because damage formation and BER can be restored by depletion of Abf1 or Reb1 protein from the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from anchor-away experiments.

claim: The interplay between base damage formation and BER may play an important role in affecting mutation frequency in gene regulatory regions.
source: Thus, our data reveal that TF binding significantly modulates alkylation base damage formation and inhibits repair by the BER pathway. The interplay between base damage formation and BER may play an important role in affecting mutation frequency in gene regulatory regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Alkylating agents comprise a large number of reactive chemicals present in cells and in the environment.
source: Alkylating agents comprise a large number of reactive chemicals present in cells and in the environment (Fu et al., 2012), which can react with the nitrogen and oxygen atoms of DNA bases to induce formation of alkylation damage.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2012.

claim: Alkylating agents can react with the nitrogen and oxygen atoms of DNA bases to induce formation of alkylation damage.
source: Alkylating agents comprise a large number of reactive chemicals present in cells and in the environment (Fu et al., 2012), which can react with the nitrogen and oxygen atoms of DNA bases to induce formation of alkylation damage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of alkylation damage, supported by citation.

claim: Some alkylation damage is cytotoxic and mutagenic.
source: Some alkylation damage is cytotoxic and mutagenic (Kondo et al., 2010), and thus poses threats to cell growth and genome stability.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kondo et al., 2010.

claim: The cytotoxicity of DNA alkylation is utilized in chemotherapy.
source: On the other hand, the cytotoxicity of DNA alkylation is utilized in chemotherapy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer treatment.

claim: Alkylating agents such as temozolomide (TMZ) are used for the treatment of glioblastoma and other cancers.
source: Alkylating agents such as temozolomide (TMZ) are used for the treatment of glioblastoma and other cancers (Fu et al., 2012; Newlands ES, Stevens MFG, Wedge SR, Wheelhouse RT, Brock C, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2012 and Newlands et al., 1997.

claim: The most common alkylation lesions are N-methylpurines (NMPs), including 7-methylguanine (7meG) and 3-methyladenine (3meA).
source: The most common alkylation lesions are N-methylpurines (NMPs), including 7-methylguanine (7meG) and, to a lesser extent, 3-methyladenine (3meA) (Kondo et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kondo et al., 2010.

claim: 7meG is prone to spontaneous depurination to form a mutagenic apurinic (AP) site.
source: Although 7meG is not genotoxic by itself, it is prone to spontaneous depurination to form a mutagenic apurinic (AP) site (Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2012.

claim: 7meG can form deleterious DNA–protein crosslinks with the lysine-rich histone tails.
source: 7meG can also form deleterious DNA–protein crosslinks with the lysine-rich histone tails (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: 3meA lesions block DNA polymerases and affect DNA replication.
source: The 3meA damage is even more harmful than 7meG, as 3meA lesions block DNA polymerases and affect DNA replication (Plosky et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Plosky et al., 2008.

claim: The primary repair pathway for NMPs is base excision repair (BER), which is initiated by alkyladenine-DNA glycosylase (AAG) in human cells or its yeast ortholog Mag1.
source: The primary repair pathway for NMPs is base excision repair (BER), which is initiated by alkyladenine-DNA glycosylase (AAG; also known as MPG and ANPG) in human cells or its yeast ortholog Mag1 (O'Connor and Laval, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to O'Connor and Laval, 1991.

claim: During BER, AAG/Mag1 removes the alkylated base and generates an AP site, which is then cleaved by the apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease (APE1).
source: During BER, AAG/Mag1 removes the alkylated base and generates an AP site, which is then cleaved by the apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease (APE1) (Mol et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement describes the BER mechanism and is supported by a citation to Mol et al., 2000.

claim: DNA polymerase and ligase are recruited to the nick to conduct repair synthesis and ligation during BER.
source: Subsequently, DNA polymerase and ligase are recruited to the nick to conduct repair synthesis and ligation, respectively (Krokan and Bjørås, 2013).
evidence: This statement describes the BER mechanism and is supported by a citation to Krokan and Bjørås, 2013.

claim: Transcription factors (TFs) are key proteins that regulate gene expression.
source: Transcription factors (TFs) are key proteins that regulate gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TF function.

claim: Many TFs bind to DNA in a sequence-specific manner to direct transcription initiation to target promoters.
source: Many TFs bind to DNA in a sequence-specific manner to direct transcription initiation to target promoters (Jolma et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jolma et al., 2013.

claim: TF binding to DNA can affect DNA damage formation and repair.
source: While TFs mainly function in transcriptional regulation, their binding to DNA can affect DNA damage formation and repair (Mao and Wyrick, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mao and Wyrick, 2019.

claim: Several TF proteins have been shown to modulate formation of ultraviolet (UV) light-induced photolesions.
source: To this end, several TF proteins have been shown to modulate formation of ultraviolet (UV) light-induced photolesions (Frigola et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2018) and inhibit nucleotide excision repair (NER) (Conconi et al., 1999; Sabarinathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Frigola et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2018.

claim: Several TF proteins have been shown to inhibit nucleotide excision repair (NER).
source: To this end, several TF proteins have been shown to modulate formation of ultraviolet (UV) light-induced photolesions (Frigola et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2018) and inhibit nucleotide excision repair (NER) (Conconi et al., 1999; Sabarinathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Conconi et al., 1999; Sabarinathan et al., 2016.

claim: The altered UV damage formation and suppressed NER are believed to cause increased mutation rates at TF binding sites in skin cancers.
source: The altered UV damage formation and suppressed NER are believed to cause increased mutation rates at TF binding sites in skin cancers (Frigola et al., 2021; Mao et al., 2018; Sabarinathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Frigola et al., 2021; Mao et al., 2018; Sabarinathan et al., 2016.

claim: Mutation rates are significantly increased at TF binding sites in non-UV exposed tumors.
source: Previous studies have also found that mutation rates are significantly increased at TF binding sites in non-UV exposed tumors (Kaiser et al., 2016; Melton et al., 2015), such as gastric and prostate cancers (Guo et al., 2018; Morova et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kaiser et al., 2016; Melton et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2018; Morova et al., 2020.

claim: Base damage caused by endogenous and exogenous damaging sources is prevalently associated with cancer mutations.
source: Since base damage (e.g. oxidative, alkylation, uracil, and so on) caused by endogenous and exogenous damaging sources is prevalently associated with cancer mutations (Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017; Wallace et al., 2012), a potential mechanism for mutation elevation in non-UV exposed tumors is increased base damage formation and/or suppressed BER in TF-bound DNA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017; Wallace et al., 2012.

claim: A potential mechanism for mutation elevation in non-UV exposed tumors is increased base damage formation and/or suppressed BER in TF-bound DNA.
source: Since base damage (e.g. oxidative, alkylation, uracil, and so on) caused by endogenous and exogenous damaging sources is prevalently associated with cancer mutations (Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017; Wallace et al., 2012), a potential mechanism for mutation elevation in non-UV exposed tumors is increased base damage formation and/or suppressed BER in TF-bound DNA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on existing knowledge and their experimental setup.

claim: Alkylation damage has been widely used as a model lesion for BER studies.
source: Alkylation damage has been widely used as a model lesion for BER studies (Fu et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015.

claim: NMP-seq is a sequencing method developed to map 7meG and 3meA lesions across the genome.
source: NMP-seq is a sequencing method developed to map 7meG and 3meA lesions across the genome (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2017.

claim: NMP-seq employs BER enzymes AAG and APE1 to digest MMS-damaged DNA and create a nick at the NMP lesion site.
source: This method employs BER enzymes AAG and APE1 to digest MMS-damaged DNA and create a nick at the NMP lesion site, which is then ligated to adaptor DNA for next-generation sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the NMP-seq methodology and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NMP lesion sites are precisely tagged by the adaptor DNA in NMP-seq.
source: As NMP lesion sites are precisely tagged by the adaptor DNA, sequencing with a primer complementary to the adaptor generates a genome-wide profile of NMP lesions at single-nucleotide resolution (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the NMP-seq methodology and is supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2017.

claim: A total of ~44 million sequencing reads were obtained in MMS-treated mag1Δ cells.
source: We obtained a total of ~44 million sequencing reads in MMS-treated mag1Δ cells.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: The majority of the reads (~56%) were associated with G nucleotides (G reads) in MMS-treated mag1Δ cells.
source: The majority of the reads (~56%) were associated with G nucleotides (G reads), followed by A nucleotides (A reads) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with the expected trend of 7meG and 3meA lesion formation after MMS treatment (Friedberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This is experimental data from NMP-seq, supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Friedberg et al., 2006.

claim: 7meG is the major class of lesion induced by MMS.
source: Since 7meG is the major class of lesion induced by MMS, we first characterized 7meG formation at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MMS-induced damage.

claim: Formation of 7meG was significantly inhibited at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA.
source: Importantly, we found that formation of 7meG was significantly inhibited at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: 7meG was reduced by up to 40% at Abf1 binding sites.
source: Analysis of the average 7meG levels in 5 bp non-overlapping moving windows indicates that 7meG was reduced by up to 40 and 70% for Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites, respectively, and the difference is statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 7meG was reduced by up to 70% at Reb1 binding sites.
source: Analysis of the average 7meG levels in 5 bp non-overlapping moving windows indicates that 7meG was reduced by up to 40 and 70% for Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites, respectively, and the difference is statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The extent of damage reduction was correlated with the level of TF occupancy.
source: Furthermore, the extent of damage reduction was correlated with the level of TF occupancy, as Reb1 binding sites with low occupancy (occupancy <10) (Kasinathan et al., 2014) only slightly reduced 7meG formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of NMP-seq data at high and low occupancy Reb1 sites, shown in Figure 1C, and references published occupancy data from Kasinathan et al., 2014.

claim: 7meG formation was significantly suppressed in the conserved regions of the motif sequences where Abf1 and Reb1 proteins directly contact DNA.
source: This analysis shows that 7meG formation was significantly suppressed in the conserved regions of the motif sequences (Figure 1D, E) where Abf1 and Reb1 proteins directly contact DNA (Jaiswal et al., 2016; McBroom and Sadowski, 1994a).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1D, E and citations to structural studies.

claim: 7meG damage levels were not affected outside of the core motif (e.g. –20 to –10 and 10–20 bp relative to the motif midpoint).
source: In contrast, 7meG damage levels were not affected outside of the core motif (e.g. –20 to –10 and 10–20 bp relative to the motif midpoint).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data analysis.

claim: 7meG levels were relatively even across the 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites.
source: 7meG levels were relatively even across the 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites (Figure 1F), even though these sites have nearly identical motif sequence as the 'high-occupancy' binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Increased 7meG levels (~1.5 fold) were observed at a few positions (e.g. −7,–3, –2, and 0) at the edge of the Abf1 motif or between the two highly conserved regions within the motif.
source: While damage formation was mainly suppressed in the core motif, we also saw increased 7meG levels (~1.5 fold) at a few positions (e.g. −7,–3, –2, and 0) at the edge of the Abf1 motif or between the two highly conserved regions within the motif (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The reduction of damage formation was not due to deletion of the MAG1 gene.
source: Additionally, the reduction of damage formation was not due to deletion of the MAG1 gene, because 7meG formation was also inhibited at Abf1 and Reb1 sites in WT-0 h cells after normalization to damage in the naked DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from WT cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: 3meA formation was increased at the –3 position of the 'high-occupancy' Reb1 sites, but not at the same position of the 'low-occupancy' Reb1 sites.
source: Moreover, analysis of A reads indicates that 3meA formation was increased at the –3 position of the 'high-occupancy' Reb1 sites, but not at the same position of the 'low-occupancy' Reb1 sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The increased 3meA formation appears to be position dependent.
source: Intriguingly, the increased 3meA formation appears to be position dependent, because the adjacent –2 and –1 positions (both are conserved in A or T) did not show elevated 3meA damage formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMP-seq data showing differential damage at adjacent positions.

claim: Reb1 protein binding causes a large curvature (~56°) in DNA and significantly compresses the minor groove near the –3 position.
source: Analysis of the published Reb1-DNA complex structure (Jaiswal et al., 2016) indicates that Reb1 protein binding causes a large curvature (~56°) in DNA and significantly compresses the minor groove near the –3 position.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of published structural data from Jaiswal et al., 2016.

claim: Structural changes caused by Reb1 protein binding may play a role in modulating 3meA formation.
source: These structural changes caused by Reb1 protein binding may play a role in modulating 3meA formation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting structural features to damage formation.

claim: Repair of 7meG lesions was strongly suppressed at both Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites in wild-type (WT) cells.
source: Our analysis indicates that repair of 7meG lesions was strongly suppressed at both Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites in wild-type (WT) cells, shown by peaks of unrepaired damage at 1 and 2hr (Figure 2) near the TF binding midpoint.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The repair suppression is mediated by TF binding, not the underlying DNA sequence.
source: The repair suppression is mediated by TF binding, not the underlying DNA sequence, because no repair inhibition was observed at 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites (Figure 2C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of repair at high and low occupancy sites shown in Figure 2C, F.

claim: Nucleosomes around the TF binding sites play an important role in affecting 7meG repair.
source: Additionally, nucleosomes around the TF binding sites play an important role in affecting 7meG repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the repair patterns observed in relation to nucleosome positions.

claim: Fast repair was observed in the nucleosome-depleted region around the TF binding site and linker DNA between two adjacent nucleosomes.
source: Fast repair was observed in the nucleosome-depleted region around the TF binding site and linker DNA between two adjacent nucleosomes (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Slow repair was found near nucleosome peaks, which is consistent with previous studies showing inhibition of BER at the nucleosome dyad center.
source: In contrast, slow repair was found near nucleosome peaks, which is consistent with previous studies showing inhibition of BER at the nucleosome dyad center (Kennedy et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data and citations to Kennedy et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2017.

claim: BER is affected by the combined effects of TF binding and nucleosome positioning.
source: These data indicate that BER is affected by the combined effects of TF binding and nucleosome positioning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed repair patterns in relation to both TF binding and nucleosome positions.

claim: Repair was suppressed in an ~ 20–30bp DNA region for Abf1 and 'high-occupancy' Reb1, but not for 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites.
source: Analysis of the remaining damage at single-nucleotide resolution confirmed repair inhibition and further indicated that repair was suppressed in an ~ 20–30bp DNA region for Abf1 and 'high-occupancy' Reb1, but not for 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites (Figure 2G-L).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 2G-L.

claim: TF binding inhibits BER in a slightly broader DNA region (both core motif and adjacent DNA) relative to its impact on NMP damage formation (mainly in the core motif).
source: Hence, TF binding inhibits BER in a slightly broader DNA region (both core motif and adjacent DNA) relative to its impact on NMP damage formation (mainly in the core motif).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of damage formation and repair patterns.

claim: Repair of 7meG by BER is initiated by the Mag1 glycosylase in yeast.
source: Repair of 7meG by BER is initiated by the Mag1 glycosylase in yeast (Wyatt et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wyatt et al., 1999.

claim: NMP-seq analysis in the mag1Δ mutant revealed higher levels of unrepaired 7meG lesions at 2 hr than in WT.
source: NMP-seq analysis in this mutant revealed higher levels of unrepaired 7meG lesions at 2 hr than in WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with deficient BER for NMPs in the mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from mag1Δ cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in remaining damage between the TF binding sites and flanking DNA in mag1Δ cells.
source: Moreover, there was no difference in remaining damage between the TF binding sites and flanking DNA in mag1Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), confirming that BER is inhibited by TF binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from mag1Δ cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both Abf1 and Reb1 are essential for yeast survival and cannot be knocked out.
source: As both Abf1 and Reb1 are essential for yeast survival and cannot be knocked out, we used the published Anchor-Away strategy (Haruki et al., 2008) to conditionally and rapidly export the protein from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these yeast TFs, supported by citation to the Anchor-Away method.

claim: Both Abf1 and Reb1 anchor-away strains were generated and used to study their impacts on gene transcription.
source: Both Abf1 and Reb1 anchor-away strains (Abf1-AA and Reb1-AA) were generated and used to study their impacts on gene transcription (Kubik et al., 2018; Kubik et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kubik et al., 2018; Kubik et al., 2015.

claim: Growth of Abf1-AA or Reb1-AA strain was inhibited on rapamycin-containing plates.
source: Moreover, growth of Abf1-AA or Reb1-AA strain was inhibited on rapamycin-containing plates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), confirming that nuclear depletion of either protein is lethal for yeast cells (Kubik et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Kubik et al., 2015.

claim: 7meG damage formation was still suppressed at the conserved motif sequences upon rapamycin treatment in the control strain (WT-AA).
source: In the control strain (WT-AA), in which no target protein is tagged for depletion, analysis of the NMP-seq data indicates that 7meG damage formation was still suppressed at the conserved motif sequences upon rapamycin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that rapamycin itself had little effect on NMP damage formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from WT-AA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TF depletion in Abf1-AA or Reb1-AA cells restored damage formation at their corresponding binding sites.
source: However, TF depletion in Abf1-AA or Reb1-AA cells restored damage formation at their corresponding binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from Abf1-AA and Reb1-AA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Abf1 depletion increased 7meG formation at Abf1 binding sites to a level comparable to the flanking DNA.
source: For example, Abf1 depletion increased 7meG formation at Abf1 binding sites to a level comparable to the flanking DNA; however, no damage restoration was seen at Reb1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No damage restoration was seen at Reb1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells.
source: For example, Abf1 depletion increased 7meG formation at Abf1 binding sites to a level comparable to the flanking DNA; however, no damage restoration was seen at Reb1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Damage was restored at Reb1 binding sites in Reb1-AA cells, but not at Abf1 sites.
source: Similarly, damage was restored at Reb1 binding sites in Reb1-AA cells, but not at Abf1 sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq data from Reb1-AA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nuclear depletion of each TF specifically affects damage formation at its own binding sites, but has no effect on the binding sites of the other TF.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that nuclear depletion of each TF specifically affects damage formation at its own binding sites, but has no effect on the binding sites of the other TF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of damage restoration observed in the anchor-away experiments.

claim: No repair inhibition was seen at Abf1 binding sites when Abf1 was depleted.
source: Compared to the control WT-AA strain (Figure 3A, B), no repair inhibition was seen at Abf1 binding sites when Abf1 was depleted (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BER was faster at Abf1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA in Abf1-AA cells.
source: Instead, BER was faster at Abf1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA in Abf1-AA cells (Figure 3C), likely because these binding sites are located in nucleosome-depleted regions and damage is efficiently repaired by BER (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 3C and citation to Mao et al., 2017.

claim: Repair in the surrounding nucleosomes was affected by Abf1 depletion, potentially due to the weakened nucleosome organization around Abf1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells.
source: Repair in the surrounding nucleosomes was also affected by Abf1 depletion (compare Figure 3A, C), potentially due to the weakened nucleosome organization around Abf1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells (Kubik et al., 2018), further supporting that BER is affected by TF binding and the accompanying chromatin organization.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of repair patterns and citation to Kubik et al., 2018.

claim: Repair of 7meG damage was still inhibited at Reb1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells.
source: Repair of 7meG damage was still inhibited at Reb1 binding sites in Abf1-AA cells (Figure 3D), consistent with Reb1 protein binding to its target sites in Abf1-AA cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 3D.

claim: BER was inhibited at Abf1 binding sites in Reb1-AA cells.
source: Similar results were also observed in Reb1-AA cells, where BER was inhibited at Abf1 binding sites (Figure 3E) but accelerated at Reb1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Reb1-AA cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: BER was accelerated at Reb1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA in Reb1-AA cells.
source: Similar results were also observed in Reb1-AA cells, where BER was inhibited at Abf1 binding sites (Figure 3E) but accelerated at Reb1 binding sites relative to the flanking DNA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Reb1-AA cells shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Removal of Abf1 and Reb1 exposes their target sites to the damaging chemical and BER enzymes.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that removal of Abf1 and Reb1 exposes their target sites to the damaging chemical and BER enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the restoration of damage formation and repair upon TF depletion.

claim: Abf1 and Reb1 bind to the nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of gene promoters to facilitate transcription.
source: Abf1 and Reb1 bind to the nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) of gene promoters to facilitate transcription (Kubik et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kubik et al., 2018.

claim: BER was generally faster in NDR relative to the coding region where DNA is organized into nucleosomes.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, BER (average of all genes) was generally faster in NDR relative to the coding region where DNA is organized into + 1, + 2, and so on nucleosomes (Figure 4A), a pattern consistent with our previous studies (Mao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 4A and citation to Mao et al., 2017.

claim: The global BER pattern indicates that Abf1 and Reb1 do not inhibit repair in NDR when all genes were included.
source: Hence, the global BER pattern revealed by our analysis indicates that Abf1 and Reb1 do not inhibit repair in NDR when all genes were included.
evidence: This is an inference based on the global repair pattern observed when all genes are analyzed together.

claim: A prominent damage peak was found in NDR after 2 hr repair in WT cells for Abf1-linked and Reb1-linked genes.
source: For each subset of genes (i.e. Abf1- or Reb1-linked genes), we found a prominent damage peak in NDR after 2 hr repair in WT cells (Figure 4B, C, black arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: The damage peak was located ~ 100 bp upstream of the TSS and overlapped with Abf1 or Reb1 binding peak.
source: The damage peak was located ~ 100 bp upstream of the TSS and overlapped with Abf1 or Reb1 binding peak (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene-by-gene analysis revealed a strong correlation between BER inhibition and TF binding.
source: Our gene-by-gene analysis revealed a strong correlation between BER inhibition (i.e. high remaining damage) and TF binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that Abf1 and Reb1 inhibit BER in their target genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by heat map analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of Abf1 in Abf1-AA cells did not change the global BER pattern when all genes were included.
source: We found that depletion of Abf1 in Abf1-AA cells did not change the global BER pattern when all genes were included (Figure 4D), but it restored repair in the NDR of Abf1 target genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Depletion of Abf1 restored repair in the NDR of Abf1 target genes.
source: We found that depletion of Abf1 in Abf1-AA cells did not change the global BER pattern when all genes were included (Figure 4D), but it restored repair in the NDR of Abf1 target genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Repair in Reb1 target genes was still inhibited in the Abf1-AA cells.
source: As expected, repair in Reb1 target genes was still inhibited in the Abf1-AA cells (Figure 4F, black arrow).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data from Abf1-AA cells shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 3meA has long been known to be cytotoxic.
source: Although 3meA is much less abundant than 7meG in MMS-treated cells, 3meA has long been known to be cytotoxic (Fu et al., 2012; Plosky et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2012; Plosky et al., 2008.

claim: Conventional methods studying cellular repair of MMS-induced damage cannot distinguish repair of 7meG and 3meA.
source: Conventional methods studying cellular repair of MMS-induced damage (e.g. AAG/APE1 digestion followed by gel electrophoresis) (Czaja et al., 2014) cannot distinguish repair of 7meG and 3meA.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Czaja et al., 2014.

claim: 3meA is unstable and difficult to be synthesized in vitro.
source: Additionally, 3meA is unstable and difficult to be synthesized in vitro.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the properties of 3meA.

claim: The repair of 3meA was inhibited near the center of Abf1 and 'high-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites.
source: Analysis of 3meA lesions in WT cells indicates that the repair was inhibited near the center of Abf1 and 'high-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites, as shown by high levels of remaining 3meA lesions at 2 hr (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: 3meA repair was not inhibited at 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites.
source: In contrast, 3meA repair was not inhibited at 'low-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The 3meA peaks appear to be narrower than the 7meG peaks.
source: Interestingly, the 3meA peaks appear to be narrower than the 7meG peaks, and no clear 3meA repair inhibition was seen in nucleosomes surrounding the TF binding sites.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of 3meA and 7meG repair data.

claim: No clear 3meA repair inhibition was seen in nucleosomes surrounding the TF binding sites.
source: Interestingly, the 3meA peaks appear to be narrower than the 7meG peaks, and no clear 3meA repair inhibition was seen in nucleosomes surrounding the TF binding sites.
evidence: This is an observation based on NMP-seq repair data.

claim: These differences are consistent with the greater activity of Mag1 and its homologs in removing 3meA than 7meG.
source: These differences are consistent with the greater activity of Mag1 and its homologs in removing 3meA than 7meG (Connor et al., 2005), which may lead to less repair inhibition to 3meA lesions by DNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on known enzyme activity from Connor et al., 2005.

claim: A slow repair spot was found at the +4 position of 'high-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites for 3meA.
source: A closer examination of 3meA repair at 'high-occupancy' Reb1 binding sites revealed a slow repair spot at the +4 position (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Repair of 7meG was also inhibited at the +4 position of Reb1 binding sites.
source: Repair of 7meG was also inhibited at the same location (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the +4 position is refractory to BER enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The +4 position is directly contacted by the DNA binding domain of Reb1 protein.
source: Although the sequence at +4 position is not conserved in the Reb1 motif, the Reb1–DNA crystal structure (Jaiswal et al., 2016) shows that this position is directly contacted by the DNA binding domain of Reb1 protein.
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of the published crystal structure from Jaiswal et al., 2016.

claim: Inosine can naturally arise from adenine deamination in cells and is repaired by AAG-mediated BER.
source: Inosine can naturally arise from adenine deamination in cells and is repaired by AAG-mediated BER (Alseth et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alseth et al., 2014.

claim: Inosine incorporation did not significantly change Reb1 binding affinity compared to DNA without inosine.
source: We found that inosine incorporation did not significantly change Reb1 binding affinity compared to DNA without inosine (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Quantification of the gels showed significantly reduced repair activity at the binding site in Reb1-bound DNA relative to the naked DNA substrate.
source: Quantification of the gels showed significantly reduced repair activity at the binding site in Reb1-bound DNA relative to the naked DNA substrate (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro BER assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Reduced BER activity was also observed when inosine was placed on the other strand at the + 4 position.
source: Reduced BER activity was also observed when inosine was placed on the other strand at the + 4 position (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro BER assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In vitro data indicate that BER of DNA base damage is suppressed by TF binding.
source: Hence, these in vitro data, consistent with our cellular damage sequencing data, indicate that BER of DNA base damage is suppressed by TF binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on both in vitro and cellular data.

claim: TF binding has been shown to inhibit NER of UV damage.
source: TF binding has been shown to inhibit NER of UV damage (Frigola et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2017); however, it is not known if NER and BER are inhibited to the same extent.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Frigola et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2017.

claim: Formation of UV-induced CPDs is significantly suppressed at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites.
source: Using a UV damage mapping method cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer sequencing (CPD-seq), we previously showed that formation of UV-induced CPDs is significantly suppressed at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites (Mao et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mao et al., 2016.

claim: Repair of CPDs at 2 hr was inhibited at both Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites in WT cells.
source: We found that repair of CPDs at 2 hr (normalized to CPDs at 0 hr) was inhibited at both Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites in WT cells, shown by high levels of unrepaired CPDs at the binding sites relative to the flanking nucleosome-occupied DNA (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CPD-seq repair data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: GG-NER was suppressed at the center of Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites, but elevated in DNA adjacent to the center due to depletion of nucleosomes.
source: Our data indicates that GG-NER was suppressed at the center of Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites, but elevated in DNA adjacent to the center due to depletion of nucleosomes (Figure 6C, D), similar to the BER pattern (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CPD-seq repair data from rad26Δ cells shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: GG-NER was also modulated by nucleosomes positioned around the TF binding sites.
source: Additionally, GG-NER was also modulated by nucleosomes positioned around the TF binding sites.
evidence: This is an observation based on CPD-seq repair data.

claim: GG-NER is inhibited by both Abf1 and Reb1 at their binding sites.
source: These analyses indicate that GG-NER is inhibited by both Abf1 and Reb1 at their binding sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on CPD-seq repair data.

claim: GG-NER was inhibited in a broader DNA region at Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites compared to BER.
source: A comparison between CPD and 7meG repair indicates that GG-NER was inhibited in a broader DNA region at Abf1 and Reb1 binding (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of CPD-seq and NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 6E, F.

claim: BER was inhibited in ~ 30 bp DNA surrounding the center of the binding motif.
source: While BER (i.e. 7meG repair) was inhibited in ~ 30 bp DNA surrounding the center of the binding motif, inhibition of GG-NER was extended by an additional 10 bp on each side (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of repair data shown in Figure 6E, F.

claim: Inhibition of GG-NER was extended by an additional 10 bp on each side compared to BER.
source: While BER (i.e. 7meG repair) was inhibited in ~ 30 bp DNA surrounding the center of the binding motif, inhibition of GG-NER was extended by an additional 10 bp on each side (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of repair data shown in Figure 6E, F.

claim: High-resolution sequencing data demonstrate the difference between BER and GG-NER at TF binding sites.
source: These high-resolution sequencing data demonstrate the difference between BER and GG-NER at TF binding sites, which is consistent with the different mechanisms underling NER and BER (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of NMP-seq and CPD-seq data.

claim: TF binding can significantly modulate NMP damage formation.
source: Our data shows that TF binding can significantly modulate NMP damage formation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NMP-seq damage formation data.

claim: The highly conserved nucleotides in the core motif of both Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites mainly suppressed NMP damage formation.
source: The highly conserved nucleotides in the core motif of both Abf1 and Reb1 binding sites mainly suppressed NMP damage formation (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq damage formation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: NMP damage is formed via the chemical reaction between the alkylating agent and individual nucleotides.
source: NMP damage is formed via the chemical reaction between the alkylating agent and individual nucleotides (Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2012.

claim: Nucleotides with restrained reactivity with MMS will be less sensitive and thus generate reduced amounts of damage.
source: Due to protein–DNA interactions, nucleotides with restrained reactivity with MMS will be less sensitive and thus generate reduced amounts of damage.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of damage suppression.

claim: The highly conserved nucleotides in the Abf1 and Reb1 motifs are directly contacted by specific amino acids of the protein.
source: The highly conserved nucleotides in the Abf1 and Reb1 motifs are directly contacted by specific amino acids of the protein (Jaiswal et al., 2016; McBroom and Sadowski, 1994a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jaiswal et al., 2016; McBroom and Sadowski, 1994a.

claim: Abf1 and Reb1 reduce the reactivity of the bound nucleotides, thus protecting conserved parts of the core motif from alkylation DNA damage.
source: This suggests that Abf1 and Reb1 reduce the reactivity of the bound nucleotides, thus protecting conserved parts of the core motif from alkylation DNA damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed damage suppression and protein-DNA contacts.

claim: The protective role of TFs does not seem be specific for alkylation damage.
source: The protective role of TFs does not seem be specific for alkylation damage.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with UV damage studies.

claim: UV damage formation was reported to be suppressed by TF binding in yeast and human cells.
source: UV damage formation was also reported to be suppressed by TF binding in yeast (Mao et al., 2016) and human cells (Frigola et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mao et al., 2016 and Frigola et al., 2021.

claim: TF binding may function as an important mechanism in cells that protects conserved regulatory sequences from being damaged and mutated.
source: Thus, TF binding may function as an important mechanism in cells that protects conserved regulatory sequences from being damaged and mutated.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: TF binding-mediated DNA structural change plays a critical role in dictating UV damage yields.
source: While the detailed mechanism for elevated alkylation damage formation is unclear, previous studies of UV damage formation revealed that TF binding-mediated DNA structural change plays a critical role in dictating damage yields.
evidence: This statement is based on previous studies of UV damage.

claim: Human ETS TFs have been shown to change the DNA geometry at their binding sites and cause individual UV damage and mutation hotspots.
source: Indeed, human ETS (E26 transformation-specific) TFs have been shown to change the DNA geometry at their binding sites and cause individual UV damage and mutation hotspots (Elliott et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2018.

claim: Yeast Abf1 protein has been shown to bend DNA toward its minor groove.
source: Yeast Abf1 protein has been shown to bend DNA toward its minor groove (McBroom and Sadowski, 1994b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McBroom and Sadowski, 1994b.

claim: DNA bending caused by Abf1 may expose certain bases in the motif and increase their reactivity with MMS, resulting in elevated damage yields.
source: DNA bending caused by Abf1 may expose certain bases in the motif and increase their reactivity with MMS, resulting in elevated damage yields.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed damage hotspots.

claim: The DNA-binding domain (DBD) of Reb1 winds around two turns of duplex DNA as a series of four helix-turn-helix (HTH) domains, forming a 'saddle'-shaped structure.
source: The DNA-binding domain (DBD) of Reb1 winds around two turns of duplex DNA as a series of four helix-turn-helix (HTH) domains, forming a so-called "saddle"-shaped structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the published Reb1-DNA complex structure.

claim: Positions +2–0 (i.e., GGG) are directly bound by both MybAD2 and MybR1 and exhibit significantly reduced 7meG formation.
source: Within the central core of the Reb1 consensus (5'-GGGTAA-3'; the underlined G is position 0), positions +2–0 (i.e., GGG) are directly bound by both MybAD2 and MybR1 and exhibit significantly reduced 7meG formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim integrates structural analysis with NMP-seq damage data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The minor groove from positions –1 to –3 is strongly compressed in width and increased in depth in the Reb1-DNA complex.
source: Positions –1 to –3 (i.e. TAA) are sandwiched between the subsites for MybAD1 and MybAD2, which insert recognition helices into the adjacent DNA major groove. As a result, the minor groove from positions –1 to –3 is strongly compressed in width and increased in depth (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Preferential formation of 3meA at position –3 may be facilitated by enhanced minor groove narrowing and DNA curvature by Reb1 binding.
source: These results suggest that preferential formation of 3meA at position –3 may be facilitated by enhanced minor groove narrowing and DNA curvature by Reb1 binding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting structural features to damage formation.

claim: The strong binding of DBD leads to significantly slower BER kinetics in the central core of Reb1 binding sites.
source: As expected, the strong binding of DBD leads to significantly slower BER kinetics in the central core, as shown by little change of 7meG damage levels after 1 or 2 hr repair compared to the initial damage at 0 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim integrates structural understanding with NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nucleotides in the flanking DNA are bound by the Reb1 protein.
source: In addition to the core motif, the structural data indicates that nucleotides in the flanking DNA are bound by the Reb1 protein (Jaiswal et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is based on structural data from Jaiswal et al., 2016.

claim: BER in the flanking regions (e.g. –12 to –4 and +4 to +12) was inhibited at Reb1 binding sites.
source: Consistently, BER in the flanking regions (e.g. –12 to –4 and +4 to +12) was also inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMP-seq repair data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is conceivable that Abf1 also binds to both the core motif and part of the flanking DNA.
source: Although Abf1–DNA complex structure data is currently unavailable, it is conceivable that Abf1 also binds to both the core motif and part of the flanking DNA.
evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy with Reb1.

claim: The strength of protein–DNA interaction in the flanking DNA may not be as high as in the core motif, which still allows damage formation to occur, but considerably reduces the access of BER enzymes.
source: The strength of protein–DNA interaction in the flanking DNA may not be as high as in the core motif, which still allows damage formation to occur, but it considerably reduces the access of BER enzymes, particularly in DNA immediately adjacent to the core motif.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed patterns of damage and repair.

claim: Damage hotspots induced by TF binding cannot be efficiently repaired and may eventually cause individual mutation hotspots when DNA is replicated.
source: As BER is generally inhibited in TF-bound DNA, damage hotspots induced by TF binding cannot be efficiently repaired and may eventually cause individual mutation hotspots when DNA is replicated.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the mutagenic consequences of the findings.

claim: The findings provide a potential explanation to mutation hotspots at TF binding sites in non-UV exposed tumors.
source: Considering the conserved damage formation and repair mechanisms between yeast and human cells, our findings provide a potential explanation to mutation hotspots at TF binding sites in non-UV exposed tumors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the relevance to human cancer.

claim: AAG-mediated BER pathway plays a direct role in affecting RNA Pol II transcription.
source: Moreover, recent studies suggest that AAG-mediated BER pathway plays a direct role in affecting RNA Pol II transcription (Montaldo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Montaldo et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations at TF binding sites may affect gene expression in cells exposed to alkylating agents.
source: This, in combination with mutations at TF binding sites, may affect gene expression in cells exposed to alkylating agents.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the functional consequences.

claim: The affected DNA region is considerably broader in NER compared to BER at TF binding sites.
source: The comparison between NMP and CPD repair at TF binding sites provides new insights into how TFs affect BER and NER differently. While TF binding inhibits both BER and NER, we found that the affected DNA region is considerably broader in NER compared to BER.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of NMP-seq and CPD-seq data.

claim: NER is inhibited in about 50 bp DNA centered on the midpoint of Abf1 or Reb1 binding sites.
source: NER is inhibited in about 50 bp DNA centered on the midpoint of Abf1 or Reb1 binding sites, whereas BER is suppressed in a narrower DNA region (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of repair data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The extended inhibition region in NER is consistent with more proteins being involved in NER compared to BER and more stable multi-protein complex assembled on DNA for NER.
source: The extended inhibition region in NER is consistent with more proteins being involved in NER compared to BER and more stable multi-protein complex assembled on DNA for NER.
evidence: This is an inference based on known differences between NER and BER mechanisms.

claim: NER requires repair endonucleases to cleave upstream of the 5' side and downstream of the 3' side relative to the lesion, releasing a repair intermediate of ~ 25 nt.
source: Moreover, NER requires repair endonucleases to cleave upstream of the 5' side and downstream of the 3' side relative to the lesion, releasing a repair intermediate of ~ 25 nt (Huang et al., 1992; Schärer, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Huang et al., 1992; Schärer, 2013.

claim: Although UV damage located outside of the TF binding site may be recognizable by the damage recognition factor, one of the two repair cleavage sites may still be located within the binding motif and is inaccessible to the repair endonuclease.
source: Although UV damage located outside of the TF binding site may be recognizable by the damage recognition factor such as XPC or yeast Rad4, one of the two repair cleavage sites may still be located within the binding motif and is inaccessible to the repair endonuclease.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of NER inhibition.

claim: The unique 'dual-incision' mechanism of NER is consistent with the broader repair-resistant DNA region around a TF binding site compared to BER.
source: Hence, the unique 'dual-incision' mechanism of NER is consistent with the broader repair-resistant DNA region around a TF binding site compared to BER.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the NER mechanism to the observed repair patterns.

claim: High-resolution alkylation damage and BER maps at yeast TF binding sites allow elucidation of how TF binding modulates base damage formation and repair.
source: In summary, we generated high-resolution alkylation damage and BER maps at yeast TF binding sites, which allows us to elucidate how TF binding modulates base damage formation and repair.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contributions.

claim: There is a potential connection between base damage, BER, and mutations in non-UV exposed tumors.
source: Considering the potential connection between base damage, BER, and mutations in non-UV exposed tumors, these analyses provide important insights into cancer mutations frequently elevated at TF binding sites.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the relevance to cancer.
